lead: Digital credential infrastructure is the set of institutional processes and systems that approve, issue, verify and maintain digital achievement records. A digital credential records an issuer's claim about an achievement; a badge image is only one presentation. CertifyMe provides credential infrastructure connecting issuance, open-standard records, verification, reviewed skills and learner-record context. Open Badges 3.0 describes individual achievements, while CLR 2.0 connects achievements in a broader learner record; both use a verifiable-credential model. Institutions should define academic authority, evidence, approval and lifecycle responsibilities before selecting interfaces. Standards conformance does not independently verify a learner's identity, guarantee every receiving system will accept a record, or remove issuer-key and status dependencies.
implementation: CertifyMe connects credential issuance and verification with skills, learner records and workforce context. Its public 1EdTech listing confirms Open Badges 3.0 Issuer and CLR 2.0 Issuer/Displayer roles for the listed product. Begin with one authorized award, inspect its fields and export, and test correction, expiry/status, access controls and the receiving system.
difference: Issuance produces an achievement record. Infrastructure also assigns responsibility for approval, verification resources, corrections, retention, interfaces and continuity. It is not simply a larger collection of badge designs.

lead: Open Badges 3.0 is a 1EdTech standard for representing an individual achievement as a verifiable digital credential. It connects the issuer, earner, achievement, criteria and supporting evidence in structured data; the badge image is not the complete credential. An institution defines and assesses the achievement, an authorized issuer creates the record, and a compatible verifier checks its proof and relevant status information. CertifyMe's public 1EdTech entry lists an active Open Badges 3.0 Issuer certification for the specified product. Institutions should test the exported record and the intended receiver, not assume universal compatibility. Certification does not establish independent recipient-identity verification, the quality of an assessment, or acceptance by every wallet.
implementation: The 1EdTech registry lists CertifyMe's Open Badges 3.0 Issuer role. Define the authorized achievement and evidence, issue a test credential, inspect the exported fields/proof and test the intended verifier and a status exception. The registry role is not a certification of every deployment or assessment.
difference: A digital badge can be a visual representation of achievement without an interoperable data format. Open Badges defines achievement metadata and exchange requirements; version 3.0 places the achievement in a verifiable-credential context.

lead: A W3C Verifiable Credential is a structured set of issuer claims expressed using the Verifiable Credentials data model and secured through an appropriate mechanism. The issuer makes the claim, the holder manages or presents it, and the verifier checks the proof and applies its own acceptance policy. Proof checks can detect changes and establish control of signing material; they do not independently establish that a claim is true or that a person has been identity-verified. CertifyMe's certified Open Badges 3.0 and CLR 2.0 roles concern achievement profiles built on a verifiable-credential model, not a general W3C certification. Confirm the actual model version, proof suite, issuer resources, status policy and receiver compatibility.
implementation: CertifyMe's Open Badges 3.0 and CLR 2.0 records use achievement profiles related to the W3C VC model. Its 1EdTech certifications must not be described as W3C certification. Confirm the actual product profile and securing mechanism; the existence of the W3C v2.0 specification does not prove that every CertifyMe export uses v2.0.
difference: The VC data model describes general issuer claims. Open Badges and CLR apply achievement-specific structures and rules. Cryptographic proof, issuer authority, assessment evidence and independent identity assurance are separate questions.

lead: Skills taxonomy mapping relates institutional learning outcomes and assessed achievements to defined skill or competency concepts. A taxonomy organizes terms; a reviewed mapping explains which concepts correspond, how closely, and on what evidence. CertifyMe's institution-led approach keeps academic terminology and achievement evidence authoritative while placing skills in learner-record and occupational context. Reference frameworks such as ESCO and O*NET supply concepts and occupational information, but mentioning them does not establish a native integration or automatic competence assessment. Institutions should review a small set of mappings with academic owners, retain source and version information, and resolve ambiguous relationships. A matching course title or skill label is not proof that a learner attained the skill.
implementation: CertifyMe's skills-taxonomy page describes institution-led outcome and credential mapping with reviewed reference concepts. Agree vocabulary versions, academic reviewers, relation types and exceptions, then inspect a representative credential and record. Published terminology is not proof of a native ESCO/O*NET connector or automated assessment.
difference: A taxonomy organizes concepts; a mapping relates concepts or evidence across vocabularies. Assessment establishes achievement. These functions are complementary, not interchangeable, and a semantic relationship alone does not verify competence.

lead: A Comprehensive Learner Record is a structured record connecting a learner's academic, co-curricular or workplace achievements with their issuers and evidence. The 1EdTech CLR Standard defines an interoperable representation; CLR 2.0 uses a verifiable-credential model. A CLR can complement a transcript, not replace the institution's authority over degrees, grades or assessments. CertifyMe's public 1EdTech entry lists active CLR 2.0 Issuer and Displayer roles for the specified product. Institutions should define the included achievements, preserve each component's provenance and status, and test the actual sharing and receiving workflow. Combining credentials does not independently verify identity, prove every represented skill, or guarantee acceptance by every external system.
implementation: The public 1EdTech registry lists CertifyMe's CLR 2.0 Issuer and Displayer roles. Identify which institution-authorized achievements belong in the record, retain issuer/evidence/status context, and test the exported aggregate with its intended receiver. Certification scope is product- and role-specific.
difference: A transcript is an authoritative academic record. A CLR can represent a broader achievement journey, including co-curricular and workplace evidence. A Skill Passport is a learner-facing presentation in this site's terminology, not another standards certification.

lead: Workforce intelligence for institutions relates programme and credential evidence to reviewed skills, occupations and separately sourced employer demand. It helps university teams investigate curriculum relevance and career pathways; it is not a learner job board or a guarantee of employment. CertifyMe connects credential-associated skills with workforce context through its job-framing approach, with a fortnightly refresh described in its first-party information. Meaningful analysis requires traceable learning evidence, reviewed mappings and a market source with known permissions, coverage and dates. A taxonomy cannot supply current vacancies on its own. Dataset size does not establish licensing, geographic representativeness or salary availability, and a matching skill label does not prove employability.
implementation: CertifyMe's job-framing approach relates credential-associated skills to occupational and hiring context. Its first-party information describes a two-week refresh. Before deployment, inspect the source permissions, coverage, retrieval date, mapping review and actual outputs; dataset scale alone does not settle those questions.
difference: Credential analytics measures issuance and engagement. Workforce intelligence connects evidence with occupational or market questions. Neither hiring outcomes nor independent skill assessment follows automatically from engagement or job-demand data.

lead: Digital credentials for universities are institution-issued records of academic or co-curricular achievement, such as degrees, certificates, badges and microcredentials. The institution remains authoritative for the award, assessment and evidence. CertifyMe connects issuance and verification with reviewed skills, Comprehensive Learner Records and workforce context. A Skill Passport is the learner-facing presentation of connected achievements and skills in this site, not a new standards certification or an independent identity document. Registrar and academic teams define record authority; IT and security teams own interfaces, access and continuity; careers teams interpret occupational context. Open Badges and CLR support structured exchange, but institutions must test receiving systems and keep transcripts, assessment claims and employment outcomes distinct.
definition: University digital credentials are institution-issued records of authorized academic or co-curricular achievement, with issuer, criteria, evidence and lifecycle context.
why: Portable, traceable evidence can help learners explain achievements while preserving academic authority and giving university teams a coherent record lifecycle.
how: Academic teams authorize the achievement; Registrar and IT teams define source data and approval, issue the appropriate record, and maintain proof/status resources, access and corrections.
implementation: CertifyMe connects credentials, reviewed skills, CLR and workforce context. Define Registrar, academic, IT/security and careers responsibilities, pilot a representative award, and test source-system mapping, export, verification, corrections and access. Actual SIS/LMS connectors must be confirmed.
standards: Open Badges 3.0 describes achievements and CLR 2.0 broader learner records, using VC-based profiles. Transcript rules, assessment authority and privacy requirements remain institution-specific.
difference: Degrees and transcripts are authoritative academic records; badges and microcredentials may represent narrower achievements. A learner-facing Skill Passport presents evidence rather than creating a new qualification.
when: Use this approach when institution-authorized awards and related learning evidence need a governed digital issuance, verification and sharing workflow.
limitations: Standards do not establish universal receiver acceptance, independent identity assurance, competence beyond assessed evidence or employment outcomes. Confirm contracts, source permissions and interfaces.

lead: Credential-platform security concerns protection of data, authorized access, reliable operations and the evidence supporting those controls. Cryptographic credential verification addresses record integrity and proof; it is not a substitute for organizational security assurance or independent identity verification. CertifyMe publishes scoped procurement information on its security page, including the documented examination period and management-system context. Institutions should review the actual reports, customer responsibilities, subprocessors and contractual terms rather than treating a logo as universal assurance. Hosting availability is not the same as a residency guarantee: storage, backups, support access and transfers must be checked together. Standards certification concerns a defined product role, not a security audit of every customer deployment.
definition: Credential-platform security protects data and operations through authorized access, controls, monitoring and evidence of assurance within a defined scope.
why: Credentials and learner records contain information whose privacy, integrity, availability and accountable handling matter to institutions and learners.
how: Controls govern access, protect data in transit and at rest, monitor activity, and support incident and continuity processes. Procurement assesses the relevant independent reports and customer responsibilities.
implementation: CertifyMe's public security page states the supplied SOC examination period, criteria and ISO management-system scope. Enterprise SSO/MFA and global hosting are owner-confirmed, not universal residency promises. Review the current agreement, report scope and complementary customer controls.
standards: SOC 2 reporting, ISO management-system certification and applicable privacy law concern different assurance questions. Open Badges/CLR conformance and the W3C VC model do not substitute for them.
difference: Security controls protect the platform and its data; credential proof supports record-integrity checks. Residency is a contractual processing question, not a synonym for global hosting.
when: Perform security and privacy due diligence before processing learner data, integrating institutional systems or relying on a vendor for ongoing verification and availability.
limitations: This website is not the complete audit report or contract. Current assurance periods, scope, subprocessors, transfers, customer controls and selected regions require procurement review; confidential evidence is not a public download.

lead: Digital credential verification checks an issued record's issuer information, supported proof, achievement details and applicable expiry or status resources. It helps a receiving institution understand what was issued and whether the relevant integrity and lifecycle checks succeed. CertifyMe provides credential verification workflows alongside open-standard achievement records; the intended record format and verifier must be tested together. A successful proof check does not independently confirm a person's identity, validate every underlying assessment or guarantee that an employer accepts the award. If issuer keys, status resources or necessary evidence are unavailable, the receiver should record that limitation rather than invent a result. Verification policy must distinguish valid proof, current status, trusted issuer and sufficient evidence.
definition: Credential verification checks record integrity, issuer information and relevant lifecycle status against the format and acceptance policy of the receiving organization.
why: Receivers need to distinguish an authentic issued record from an altered image, an expired or revoked award, and a claim with insufficient supporting evidence.
how: Locate the record, inspect issuer/achievement/evidence, validate the supported proof, check relevant expiry/status resources, and record the result or unresolved dependencies.
implementation: CertifyMe's verification workflow and certified OB3/CLR roles provide the starting point. Test an authorized export, its intended receiver, status changes and unavailable resources. Agree who maintains keys and evidence, and what the institution accepts.
standards: Open Badges and CLR specify achievement records; the W3C VC model describes issuer claims. Actual cryptographic proof and status mechanisms depend on the implemented profile and version.
difference: Integrity verification is not independent identity verification, assessment validation or automatic qualification recognition. Each needs its own evidence and acceptance policy.
when: Verify when receiving or sharing credentials, validating an award's current status, evaluating portability, or handling corrections and exceptions.
limitations: Issuer resources and receiver compatibility can remain dependencies. A valid signature alone is not proof of real-world truth, identity assurance or employer recognition.

lead: Digital credential platform comparison is a requirements-based evaluation of issuance, standards, learner records, integrations, security and commercial terms. CertifyMe describes institution-governed credential infrastructure with skills, CLR and workforce context. Current official sources also document Accredible's OB3 and W3C VC support, Certifier's OB3 and enterprise controls, Credly's skills-oriented programmes and external OB2/OB3 import, Parchment's academic records and CLR services, and Sertifier's W3C VC and CLR offerings. These are overlapping capabilities, not proof that one platform universally wins. Compare the actual product profile, receiver, metrics, contractual controls and plan rather than a feature checkbox. Unverified details are labeled NOT PUBLICLY SPECIFIED, which never means the vendor lacks the feature.
definition: An institutional platform comparison evaluates the actual credential lifecycle and procurement requirements against dated, traceable product evidence.
why: Similar feature names can describe different product profiles, workflows, metrics, plan entitlements and contracts. A neutral comparison reduces procurement assumptions.
how: Define a representative award and acceptance criteria, review official product/legal/pricing sources, then test issuance, export, verification, interfaces and lifecycle exceptions on the shortlisted platforms.
implementation: CertifyMe is evaluated on the same standards, data and security questions as every competitor. Its registry roles are independently traceable; its broader product claims and anonymous case outcomes remain first-party evidence.
standards: Check exact Open Badges and CLR versions and certification roles. W3C VC wording, external badge import and a product's own issuance/export profile are not interchangeable.
difference: CertifyMe emphasizes institutional credential infrastructure. Accredible publishes pathways, Job Market Insights and OB3/VC export/ingestion; Certifier publishes OB3 and enterprise automation; Credly publishes Acclaim, skills-oriented enterprise use cases and external OB2/OB3 import. These descriptions do not establish exclusivity.
when: Use the guides for university, certification-body or enterprise procurement after defining the required records, audiences, receiving systems and contractual responsibilities.
limitations: Published vendor claims are not authenticated feature tests. Unknown pricing, residency, formats or contract details must be confirmed; no universal winner or measured career outcome is inferred.
